title: Somatosensory input drives membrane potential dynamics in motor cortex during voluntary limb movement
experiments_summary: The study employed the following experimental methods and procedures: (1) A head-fixed forelimb reaching task was developed for water-restricted mice, using capacitive contact sensors to detect forelimb position and trigger water reward delivery. Forelimb kinematics were tracked at 500 Hz using infrared high-speed imaging of reflective markers. (2) A dorsal rhizotomy (C5–T1) was performed in a subset of trained mice (nerve-cut, NC) to remove somatosensory afferent input from the right forelimb, while leaving motor efferent output intact, and compared to intact (IT) control mice. (3) Effectiveness of nerve transection was verified using intrinsic optical imaging of cortical responses to forepaw vibrotactile stimulation (10 Hz piezoelectric stimulation, 630 nm illumination, CCD camera), comparing activation of primary somatosensory forelimb cortex (fS1) between IT and NC mice. (4) Forelimb M1 was localized using intracortical microstimulation (ICMS) in anesthetized mice, with a tungsten microelectrode inserted to 800 µm depth, delivering current pulse trains (30 ms, 333 Hz, 0–100 µA) on a 250 µm grid, combined with intrinsic optical imaging to identify fS1 relative to motor areas (CFA and RFA). (5) Pharmacological inhibition of CFA was performed by microinjecting muscimol (100 nl, 1 mM) or Ringer's solution at CFA or auditory cortex in trained mice, with reach frequency, movement duration, and grooming behavior recorded for 20 min post-injection and compared to a prior baseline session. Injection sites were confirmed post-hoc via Pontamine Sky Blue staining and histology. (6) Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings in current-clamp mode were performed in awake, head-fixed IT (n=23 mice; 11 L2/3, 11 L5 cells) and NC (n=14 mice; 10 L2/3, 12 L5 cells) mice during the forelimb task, using K-gluconate-based intracellular solution with biocytin for post-hoc cell identification. Signals were filtered at 10 kHz and digitized at 20 kHz. Laminar identity was confirmed histologically in a majority of cells. (7) Membrane potential (Vm) analysis included: averaging Vm traces aligned to movement onset, Quiet vs. Move period comparisons, Z-score analysis of pre-movement Vm timing, FFT power spectrum analysis (1–5 Hz and 30–80 Hz bands), reach-triggered averaging during Quiet and Move periods, linear regression of reach response amplitude versus pre-reach baseline Vm to estimate reach reversal potential, cross-correlation between high-pass filtered Vm and forelimb kinematic parameters (distance, speed, acceleration), and touch-triggered averaging of Vm around target sensor contact. (8) Action potential (AP) threshold was estimated from the third derivative of the Vm waveform; AP-contaminated Vm epochs were excluded and replaced with NaN for subthreshold analyses. (9) Neurons were classified as enhanced or suppressed based on mean Vm during Move versus Quiet periods, and polarity of Vm modulation around touch was classified using 200 ms windows centered on touch versus a pre-touch baseline window. (10) Histological processing included cytochrome oxidase and biocytin staining of 100 µm coronal sections, with neuronal reconstruction via NeuroLucida to confirm laminar identity. (11) Statistical analyses used non-parametric tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank, Mann–Whitney U, Z-test for proportions), Pearson correlation from linear regression, and linear mixed-effects models to control for multiple recordings per mouse.
